articles.title: Jessie Buckley suggests film industry gives too much weight to Oscar campaigns
articles.summary: The actor, who won the Academy Award for best actress this year, was speaking at the BFI and Chanel film-maker awards. Jessie Buckley has questioned whether the film industry places too much emphasis on Oscar campaigns at the expense of nurturing emerging talent, suggesting there may be greater…
body: Speaking at the BFI and Chanel film-maker awards in London, the actor was responding to comments by John Malkovich, who said Oscar campaigns were now the only way to get audiences into cinemas.

“I think there’s truth in that,” Buckley told the Guardian. “You’ve got to take responsibility for sharing your work. It would be so easy to just go and film and then hide. I wish we could all do that. But I don’t think that’s how it works any more.”
Buckley, who has made predominantly independent films, said the industry’s reliance on film promotion affected not just actors and directors but the wider workforce.
“I feel so proud of being part of this community – this affects so many people’s lives. Crews, marketing, everybody. And if you don’t support it, you’re not going to have a job,” she said.

articles.title: ‘Abbott Elementary’ Star William Stanford Davis Sets Memoir ‘Don’t Mess With the Fat Kid’ (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: William Stanford Davis, who stars in “Abbott Elementary” as the janitor Mr. Johnson, is publishing a memoir titled “Don’t Mess With the Fat Kid” via BenBella Books. “Don’t Mess With the Fat Kid” will dive into Davis’ life and career — including struggles such as addiction and rejection — and the…
body: Besides “Abbott Elementary,” Davis’ credits include the Wanda Sykes film “Undercard,” Apple TV’s “Swagger,” HBO’s “Curb Your Enthusiasm,” Showtime’s “Ray Donovan” and ABC’s “Lincoln Heights.”

“I’ve wanted to write this memoir for a long time, to honor the road I’ve taken to get here and to connect with folks who are still on their way,” Davis said in a statement. “People know me as Mr. Johnson from ‘Abbott Elementary,’ and while that’s the biggest role of my career so far, it’s not the whole story. I’m excited to finally share the full story: the struggles, the setbacks, the second chances and the perseverance it took to keep going and get to where I am today. It took me a long time to get here, and the beautiful thing is, I’m just getting started.”

body: The eight-episode show’s season finale aired on Oct. 4, and wrapped up the central mystery of who killed Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) and revealed the identity of the second Manhunter, plus how John Stewart (Aaron Pierre) becomes Earth’s sole Green Lantern in DC Studios’ forthcoming “Superman” sequel, “Man of Tomorrow.”

Before the finale, Variety reported that the show’s seventh episode reached 7 million viewers in the U.S. in its first three days of availability. Previous episodes had averaged over 12 million viewers per episode in the U.S. to date and nearly 19 million when factoring in international viewing.

articles.title: ‘Beach Fictions’ Review: Utterly Beguiling, Time-Tweaking Korean Romance Shows What a Day a Difference Makes
articles.summary: Fatalism, self-determination and imagination all gently wrestle for control of the narrative(s) in “Beach Fictions,” an enchanting and subtly profound diptych that follows one young woman through two diverging versions of the same day — saying much in the process about the voices, inner and…
body: A highlight of Busan's main competition, Lim Hayeon's artful, confident debut follows a young woman through two versions of the same timeline, steered by tellers of stories and fortune.

In the sleepy beach town, she meets and is immediately entranced by charismatic street magician Manhyuk (Kim Wookyum, delightful), only to later be warned off him by her hostess, who claims he’s a local lothario and sometime sex worker. A day in his company turns sour but when, in the film’s deftly shuffled second half, she meets him in slightly different circumstances, and the day’s events take on a different chain of connections, the potential romantic outcome differs too.

articles.title: Critics Vindicate ‘Artificial’ After Messy Amazon MGM Breakup (and the Studios vs. Talent Wars Around AI Are Just Beginning)
articles.summary: Looks like “Artificial” is the real thing. Luca Guadagnino’s genre-blending movie about the evils of artificial intelligence (and one of its fathers, Sam Altman) had a triumphant U.K. premiere at the London Film Festival on Sunday.
body: Others agree. The title has a 96% Fresh rating on review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes, representing the highest score of Guadagnino’s career across 11 feature film releases. Garfield has been catapulted to the front of the best supporting actor race, thanks to a performance that delivers “a masterclass in diabolical villainy,” according to another review.

The notices, the standing ovations, the awards buzz — all of it represents a stunning reversal of fortune for Guadagnino after the Amazon debacle in June. It was highly uncommon, in Hollywood terms, for even a tech-owned content studio to kill a project it had cradled since infancy. Neon rescued the movie with a global rights deal shortly after the Amazon rift.

“We believe that ‘Artificial’ will be better served if it were released by a different studio,” the e-commerce giant said at the time. Global press almost unanimously noted that the decision to jettison the movie came only three months after Amazon signed a significant partnership with Altman’s OpenAI (including a $50 billion investment in the company).

articles.title: Gary Waddell dies aged 74: the brilliant Australian actor who turned small roles into great ones
articles.summary: Waddell appeared in countless films and TV shows, often as rough-as-guts characters, though he was rarely given the screen time he deserved. The great Australian actor Gary Waddell – known for his gooseflesh-raising ability to portray rough-as-guts characters so real you swear you’ve met them…
body: This legitimately great film – the best ever made about heroin addiction and subculture in Australia – was famously described as “the most evil film I’ve ever seen” by Melbourne Herald critic Andrew McKay (an example of hysterical overreach if ever there was one, although, as they say, those were different times). It remains a thrilling piece of social realist cinema, full of drug-taking, petty crime and tomfoolery, with the story revolving around Waddell’s character Lou, who arrives five minutes in, grousing about how he “hasn’t had a hit for 10 hours”.

Since then, Waddell went on to appear in countless productions, usually in small albeit often high-impact roles, in TV shows such as A Country Practice, E Street, Stingers, Blue Heelers, Water Rats, Bad Cop Bad Cop, Home and Away, City Homicide, Upright and Rake. His films included The FJ Holden, Chopper, Dirty Deeds, Gettin’ Square, Black and White, Charlie’s Country, The Stranger and 2022’s The Survival of Kindness, which featured his final screen performance.

articles.title: How we lost our appetite for eat-the-rich satire
articles.summary: Tom Cruise’s latest film could lose $250m (£190m) – could one reason be that audiences are tired of Hollywood telling them what they already know about the super-rich? It seems as if nobody can decide who should shoulder most of the blame for the recent box office flop of Digger.
body: Was it the ousted Warner Bros film executives Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy, whose love of big-budget auteur cinema usually came with a hefty price tag? Or was it the marketing team, who were responsible for hiding the movie’s biggest swing from all trailers, ensuring many viewers would be left alienated from its early meta-reveal onwards?

The truthful answer is that the film’s fate was sealed long before anybody could point fingers over its failure. In the past year it’s become clear that audiences have grown tired of the worn-out cinematic trend Digger is a part of: the eat-the-rich satire.

There was a brief moment when audiences couldn’t get enough movie takedowns of the uber-wealthy, with the breakout success of Parasite inspiring Hollywood to seize upon its class-conscious themes and drag them into the west. The sustained fallout from the Covid pandemic brought issues of wealth inequality further into the spotlight, and titles as varied as Glass Onion, Saltburn, Triangle of Sadness and The Menu all spoke to the zeitgeist with their distinct, controversial takedowns of the 1%.

articles.title: Russell Brand was a 'sexual predator', prosecution alleges as rape trial begins
articles.summary: The comedian and actor faces charges including rape and sexual assault from six female complainants who have never met each other, a court is told.
body: Russell Brand was described as "ruthless" and a "sexual predator" by the prosecution at the start of his trial for rape and sexual assault on Wednesday.
The 51-year-old actor and comedian faces three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.
The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges.
Riel Karmy-Jones KC, for the prosecution, told Southwark Crown Court in London the women "did not know each other", "have never met each other" and "came forward independently of each other".

articles.title: Winter of the Crow review – Lesley Manville magnificently on edge in intriguing cold war thriller
articles.summary: Manville’s academic psychologist finds herself trapped in a tower block wasteland in 1980s Warsaw. Bizarre and surreal details add to the sinister vibe. Part cold war thriller, part Kafkaesque reverie, this movie takes us back to the sinister drear of Poland in 1981, when General Jaruzelski has…
body: Lesley Manville plays Professor Andrews, an academic clinical psychologist (like Tokarczuk) from Britain with testy, peremptory mannerisms; her indulgence is a fondness for taking Polaroid photos. She has attained a certain level of celebrity for a book on dreams, despite claiming that she never dreams herself. Andrews has been invited to give a lecture in Warsaw, during which she begins to outline views on mental illness not unlike those of Laing or Foucault; but her speech is chaotically disrupted by students shouting that Poland itself is an oppressive asylum.

It is an intriguing and disquieting movie, though one whose storytelling impulse slows a little, and perhaps the film could have benefited from closer editing – although this might have meant losing some of the bizarre and surreal details, like the live carp that people queue up to buy for food and keep in the bath.

articles.title: Sally Rooney books withdrawn in UK over Palestine Action support
articles.summary: The Irish writer is best known for novels such as Normal People, Intermezzo and Conversations With Friends.
body: Normal People author Sally Rooney has said her novels will no longer be supplied to booksellers in the UK as a result of her support for Palestine Action.
The Irish novelist said last year she intended to carry on using her royalties to support the group, which is a proscribed terrorist organisation in the UK.

In a statement to BBC News, Rooney said further publication of her work could constitute a "serious criminal offence", so she had agreed with her publisher Faber not to continue supplying her books in the UK.
"I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences," she said.

articles.title: Netflix to shed 1,000 jobs in steepest cuts since 2022
articles.summary: The cuts equate to around 6% of the streaming giant's total workforce worldwide.
body: Netflix has said it will cut 1,000 jobs globally as the streaming giant faces competition from rivals.
The cuts - the steepest since 2022 - will mainly affect its human resources, legal, product and technology teams and equates to around 6% of its total workforce.
Last month, Netflix 's co-chief executive, Ted Sarandos, told the Bloomberg Screentime summit that the company was "not growing as fast as I want us to".

The streaming industry is going through a period of consolidation following Paramount's $110bn (£83.6bn) merger with Warner Bros, the owner of HBO, while free platforms such as YouTube and TikTok continue to attract viewers.
